points: Adapted physical activity: physical activity modified in its rules, equipment, environment or instruction so that people with a disability can take part meaningfully and safely.
The aim is meaningful participation, meaning real involvement and challenge, not just a place in the group.
It covers disability sport, such as wheelchair basketball, and adapted versions of mainstream activities.
Integration: placing a participant in an existing activity and expecting them to fit in without changing the provision.
Example of integration: a wheelchair user added to a mainstream game with no change to rules, space or equipment.
Inclusion: changing the provision so that everyone can take part with appropriate challenge.
Example of inclusion: a mixed-ability sprint session where distances and start points are set for each athlete.
Inclusion puts the responsibility on the provider to adapt, rather than on the participant to fit in.

notes.b: Five stages describe how an activity is organised for participants with and without disability.
points: Open activity: everyone does the same activity under the same rules, so no adaptation is needed.
Modified activity: rules or equipment change so that everyone can take part together.
Parallel activity: participants are grouped by ability and do the same activity at different levels, such as different distances or heights.
Separate activity: a group practises apart from others for part or all of a session.
Disability sport, with reverse integration: non-disabled participants join a disability sport such as wheelchair basketball or boccia.

notes.b: STEP stands for Space, Task, Equipment and People; each can be changed to suit a participant.
points: Space: a smaller or larger playing area, or zones that limit where a participant must move.
Task: simplified rules, more time, fewer touches before a pass, or a lower target.
Equipment: larger, lighter, softer, audible or brightly coloured balls, lower nets and ramps.
People: smaller groups, matched opponents, buddies and assigned roles.
Adaptations must keep the core challenge and the central purpose of the activity; removing the challenge turns it into a different activity.
Team game, wheelchair user: a zone where the participant receives the ball, extra time in possession and a lighter ball.
Athletics, visually impaired runner: a guide runner who runs alongside and a tether linking the two athletes.
Badminton, limited mobility: a smaller court and seated play, so the participant covers less ground.
Equipment adaptations in tennis: a smaller, lighter racquet and a softer or slower ball.
Other adaptations in tennis: allowing two bounces before a return, and a smaller court.
Accessible facilities: step-free access, accessible changing rooms and sports fields that participants can reach.
Adapted equipment available for lessons and sports days.
Trained staff who can plan and deliver inclusive lessons.
Inclusive PE planning, with adaptations built into each unit rather than added on request.
Extra-curricular opportunities, such as adapted sports sessions at lunchtime or after school.
Links with disability sport clubs that bring coaches and pathways into the school.
Ways to enhance provision: specialist equipment, staff training, inclusive sports days, and a disability sport club set up within the school.
Judgement: provision works when every student can take part in a timetabled activity, not only when an adapted sport is offered as an extra.
Accessible venues and transport so that disabled people can reach sessions.
Inclusive clubs that adapt sessions for members with disabilities.
Disability sport clubs, such as wheelchair basketball clubs.
Local Sports Partnership programmes and Sports Inclusion Disability Officers who support clubs.
Gaps: the cost of membership and adapted equipment.
Gaps: limited awareness among disabled people and their families of what clubs offer.
Pathway: an inclusive club, then a disability sport club and national governing body programmes, then national squads, then Paralympic or Special Olympics competition.
Classification: Paralympic sport groups athletes with similar levels of impairment so that competition is fair.
Support for elite para-athletes: funding, specialist coaching and carding.
Special Olympics Ireland provides a separate high-level pathway for people with intellectual disability, distinct from Paralympic classification.

notes.h: Barriers on the pathway, and improvements
points: Few specialist coaches, so athletes may not get expert training at each stage.
High cost of adapted equipment, such as racing wheelchairs and running blades.
Travel to specialist centres, which may be far from home.
Improvement: more coach education in adapted sport, so clubs can train athletes from the inclusive stage.
Improvement: equipment loan schemes and grants so athletes can try adapted equipment before buying.
Improvement: regional training centres so athletes do not have to travel far.

factCards.term: Adaptations for a visually impaired runner
factCards.definition: A guide runner and a tether.

questions.prompt: Using the STEP framework, examine how a participant with a physical disability could take part in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Activity: five-a-side football, with a participant who has limited mobility in one leg and uses crutches. Space: play on a smaller pitch with a marked zone near the goal where the participant plays, so they do not need to cover the full width. Task: allow extra time on the ball, and let the participant shoot after a single touch, so the core challenge of scoring remains. Equipment: a lighter, softer ball that is easier to control while on crutches. People: a buddy who supports the participant during play, and an assigned role as a playmaker or goalkeeper so that they make real decisions. Passing, scoring and defending all remain in the game, so the activity stays competitive and keeps its central purpose, and the participant is included rather than placed in a separate game.

questions.prompt: Examine ways in which participants in adapted physical activities can be given opportunities to achieve excellence.
questions.model: Pathway: an athlete starts in an inclusive club where they play alongside others, moves to a disability sport club and national governing body programmes that provide coaching and competition, then to national squads, and finally to Paralympic or Special Olympics competition. Classification: Paralympic sport groups athletes with similar levels of impairment so that competition is fair, and athletes must be classified before they can compete. Support: elite para-athletes receive funding, specialist coaching and carding. Special Olympics Ireland provides a separate high-level pathway for people with intellectual disability. Barriers and improvements: there are few specialist coaches, so more coach education in adapted sport is needed; adapted equipment is costly, so equipment loan schemes and grants help; travel to specialist centres can be long, so regional training centres would help athletes stay close to home.

questions.prompt: Explain 'adapted physical activity' and outline two ways a school can provide for it.
questions.model: Adapted physical activity is physical activity modified in its rules, equipment, environment or instruction so that people with a disability can take part meaningfully and safely. First way: adapted equipment and accessible facilities, such as smaller, lighter racquets and accessible changing rooms, so students can take part in lessons. Second way: inclusive PE planning, in which adaptations are built into every unit and staff are trained to deliver them, so students with disabilities take part alongside their peers.
